summary: Defines a YANG module for managing virtual partitions of a network device's resources, such as VRF instances and virtual switch instances. It follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture from RFC 8342. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: One big router can act like several separate smaller routers, each with its own private rules. This document is the form used to set up and look after each of those pretend routers.

questions: how to configure virtual routing instances

what is a vrf in yang
subtitle: A YANG module for managing VRFs and virtual switch instances inside a single network device.

tldr.problem: Network devices often split their resources into several virtual routing and switching partitions, such as VRFs and virtual switch instances, and there was no standard YANG way to create them and assign interfaces to them.
tldr.mechanism: The ietf-network-instance module defines a list of network instances, each with a mount point (vrf-root, vsi-root or vv-root) for schema mount, and adds a bind-ni-name leaf to interfaces to attach them to an instance.
tldr.outcome: A device can create and delete instances with ordinary list operations, and the modules for each instance's internal routing or bridging are mounted under it instead of being defined in this module.

today: RFC 8529 is a Standards Track document, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on RFC 8528 for schema mount.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Resource Partitioning
sections.content:
RFC 8529 is the second of two modules for devices that partition their resources. Both rely on YANG Schema Mount (RFC 8528), and the model conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342).

The first kind, defined in RFC 8530, is the logical network element (LNE): a partition managed as essentially an independent network element hosted by the base device. The second kind, defined here, is the network instance (NI). It covers what are commonly called VPN Routing and Forwarding (VRF) instances and Virtual Switch Instances (VSI). Several control-plane and forwarding or bridging instances are provided by, and managed through, one physical or logical device. Configuration of each NI always goes through the device and the network instance module.
sections.eli5: Some network boxes can pretend to be several boxes at once. This document is about the pretend boxes that share one box's brain but keep their own rules.

sections.title: How Devices, LNEs and NIs Fit Together
sections.content:
The RFC considers devices that run IETF-defined protocols, such as routers, firewalls and hosts, which may be physical or virtual. A device may subdivide its resources into LNEs, and each LNE may support VRF and VSI functions, which are called NIs. Interfaces attach to the NIs.

The interface management model (RFC 8343) is affected, so this document and RFC 8530 define augmentations to the interface module. The NI model also separates two kinds of information. One relates to the device, such as the route target used when advertising VRF routes. The other relates to the internal operation of the NI, such as routing protocols (RFC 8349). This document defines device-level information and the interface assignment, and leaves internal operation to mounted modules.
sections.eli5: A big box can hold several mini boxes, and each mini box can hold several private lanes. Cables are plugged into the lanes.

sections.title: The Network Instance Module
sections.content:
The module ietf-network-instance (prefix ni) has a container network-instances with a list network-instance keyed by name. The name is a device-scoped string that is used both as an index in the module and to associate resources with an instance. Each entry also has an enabled flag (default true) and an optional description.

Two choices complete the entry. ni-type is an anchor where documents for specific NI types, such as L3VPN or L2VPN, add cases by augmentation. root-type is mandatory and offers the well-known mount points. The module also defines the bind-ni-name-failed notification for certain failures.

Both VRF and VSI work is expected to be defined elsewhere: the RFC envisions separate models specific to L3 and L2 VPN technology, and points to drafts that are works in progress.
sections.eli5: Each mini box gets a name tag, an on-off switch and a note about what it is for. Special kinds of mini boxes can add their own extra fields.

sections.title: NI Types and Well-Known Mount Points
sections.content:
NI types largely differ in the information needed in the core, top-level instance, not in what is inside the NI. So a few schemas can be shared across types. The RFC expects very few different schemas to be needed, and defines three well-known mount points, each reusable by future NI-type modules.

Documents defining new NI types should augment the network instance module with a case holding containers for configuration and state, and generally reuse one of the well-known mount points. When none is appropriate, a type-specific mount point may be defined by augmentation. The module's own descriptions say these mount points will typically not be inline-type mount points.
sections.eli5: There are three standard plug-in sockets: one for routing boxes, one for switching boxes and one for boxes that do both. New kinds of mini boxes should use them.

sections.title: Binding Interfaces and Managing Instances
sections.content:
The interface list in ietf-interfaces is flat and knows nothing about virtual instances. The module augments the interface, and its IPv4 and IPv6 containers, with a bind-ni-name leaf, a leafref to a network instance name. To assign an interface to both an LNE and an NI, it is first assigned to the LNE using RFC 8530, and then the LNE's view of the interface is assigned to an NI.

Instances are controlled with ordinary list operations. Creating a list entry instantiates a new instance, and deleting one destroys it. Once an instance exists, setting bind-ni-name to a valid name means the implementation MUST do whatever is needed to assign the interface, or give an error. A failed assignment returns error-tag operation-failed and error-app-tag ni-assignment-failed, and a meaningful error-info SHOULD be provided. Because assignment can fail after asynchronous processing, the bind-ni-name-failed notification reports later failures.
sections.eli5: To give a cable to a mini box you write the mini box's name on the cable. If the box cannot take it, you get an error message, maybe a little later.

sections.title: What Lives Inside an Instance
sections.content:
Modules that represent control-plane and data-plane information are available under the root mount point for the NI type. The shared-schema method from RFC 8528 MUST be used to identify them, and a future version could relax that. Mounted modules SHOULD have access, through schema mount parent-references, to device resources such as interfaces. The list of available modules depends on the implementation.

An implementation MAY restrict parent-referenced information to a single instance, for instance allowing references only to interfaces whose binding matches the instance's name. It MAY express that restriction in the parent-reference leaf-list, so a client can see it. Parent-referenced information is available to clients through its top-level paths only, not under the mount point.

The RFC's illustration mounts the routing management module (RFC 8349) and an OSPF module under a VRF and lets them refer to interface information.
sections.eli5: Inside each mini box live its own routing rules. The mini box may peek at the cables that were given to it, but not at everyone else's cables.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is designed to be accessed with NETCONF or RESTCONF, using SSH or TLS, with NACM (RFC 8341) restricting users. The RFC separates two concerns. Mounted modules keep their own security considerations, which are not substantively changed by sitting in an NI. The NI module itself carries network configuration and route distribution policy, which the RFC says is fundamentally no different from other interface or routing configuration.

Two writable items are called vulnerable: the /network-instances/network-instance list and the bind-network-instance-name leaves on interfaces. Unauthorized access can hurt the routing subsystem of the device and the network, leading to malfunctions or packets delivered to inappropriate destinations.
sections.eli5: Only trusted people should be allowed to rearrange the mini boxes and cables, because mistakes could send the mail to the wrong place.

sections.title: Worked Example in the Appendix
sections.content: Appendix A shows two customer-specific instances named vrf-red and vrf-blue. Each has its own router ID and an OSPF process with an interface, eth1 for red and eth2 for blue. The interface entries carry the NI binding. The appendix then gives state data for non-NMDA and NMDA servers, including the schema mount data that makes vrf-root a shared-schema mount point with a parent-reference to the interfaces module.
sections.eli5: The example sets up a red mini box and a blue mini box, each with its own route settings and its own cable.
